questions.stem: Which transport mechanism moves glucose from the tubular lumen to the epithelial cell?

evidence.quote: So, the sodium-glucose transporters, SGLT2 and SGLT1, um, those are located on the brush borders of the proximal tubule cells. Um, and again, they're, they're secondary active transporters.
Apical SGLT and NKCC2 are symporters.

questions.note:
**Glucose crosses the apical (luminal) membrane on SGLT2 and SGLT1, which are secondary active transporters riding the Na+ gradient made by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase.** The lecturer read this poll question and its five choices aloud at 00:22:52, then skipped it because the transporters hadn't been shown yet. The answer comes from slide 15 and the explanation about ten minutes later (00:32:55).

Primary active transport: false. That is the Na+/K+-ATPase itself, which spends ATP directly. It builds the gradient but doesn't carry glucose.

Secondary active transport: true. SGLTs on the brush border move glucose uphill using energy stored in the Na+ gradient.

Facilitated diffusion: false. That is how glucose leaves the cell across the basolateral membrane, through GLUT2 and GLUT1.

Simple diffusion: false. Glucose needs a carrier protein to cross either membrane.

Osmosis: false. Osmosis is water movement, not glucose.

questions.stem: If you were to see a question about anything having to do with glucose, changing the amount of glucose that either gets reabsorbed or secreted, which one do you think is going to have a bigger effect, inhibiting SGLT2 or SGLT-1?

evidence.quote: SGLT 2. OK. So if you ever see a question where some are saying like buy SGLT2, some buy SGLT1, um, you can easily eliminate SGLT1.
Um, 90% of the glucose is reabsorbed using the SGLT2, which is in the very early part of the proximal convoluted tubule.
No useful drug that inhibits SGLT-1 because it doesn't do much.
Apical SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule reabsorbs most filtered glucose.

questions.note:
**SGLT2 does about 90% of glucose reabsorption in the early proximal tubule (S1), so blocking it matters far more.** The lecturer asked this aloud with the two options built into the question and gave the answer right after. Turned into a two-choice item from that passage.

Inhibiting SGLT2: true. It carries most of the filtered glucose, which is why SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucosuria.

Inhibiting SGLT1: false. SGLT1 in the late proximal tubule (S3) only picks up the remaining ~10%. The lecturer's tip: on a question, an SGLT1 answer can almost always be eliminated.

questions.stem: A research team has developed a model to study the effect of drugs on the kidney. Their protocol involves the use of para-aminohippurate (PAH) to measure renal plasma flow at the beginning and end of the 2-week treatment period. Which of the following best describes the rationale for the use of PAH in this experiment?
choices: It is filtered and completely reabsorbed
It is filtered and partially reabsorbed
It is filtered and completely secreted
It is filtered and partially secreted
It is filtered but not absorbed nor secreted

evidence.quote: So if a substance is fully cleared from the plasma, so whatever's in your plasma, if the kidneys fully clear that and it gets excreted, then you can say your clearance rate is equal to your renal plasma flow
paraminohypuric acid is the closest thing to that, um, and it's cleared 90%.
At low plasma concentrations, filtration and proximal secretion together remove about 90% of PAH in one pass.

questions.note:
**PAH measures renal plasma flow because it is filtered and then secreted so thoroughly that almost none is left in renal venous plasma.**

A substance cleared completely from the plasma in one pass has a clearance equal to RPF. The official key treats PAH as "completely secreted"; the lecture puts the real figure at about 90%, which is why PAH clearance slightly underestimates true RPF. The idea being tested is the near-complete removal.

It is filtered and completely reabsorbed: false. That describes glucose at normal loads; its clearance is zero.

It is filtered and partially reabsorbed: false. Clearance would be below GFR, nowhere near RPF.

It is filtered and completely secreted: true. Filtration plus secretion clears (nearly) all of it, so clearance equals RPF.

It is filtered and partially secreted: false. Clearance would fall between GFR and RPF and couldn't stand in for RPF.

It is filtered but not absorbed nor secreted: false. That's inulin, the GFR marker.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man presents to his primary care office for a check up. He has a history of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus type 1. He takes insulin and occasionally takes ibuprofen for headaches. A routine urinalysis in the office is positive for the presence of glycosuria. Which of the following best explains this finding?
choices: Hyperglycemia causes increased tubular glucose secretion.
The tubular glucose concentration exceeds the Tmax for glucose reabsorption.
Tubular glucose reabsorption is inhibited by ibuprofen.
Filtration fraction for glucose is increased by ibuprofen.
Glomerular injury is leading to increased glucose filtration.

evidence.quote: up until it gets to a certain point called the transport maximum. Um, and this is where all the carrier proteins are already busy.
And that's why in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, you will see glucose in the urine. It's because you've overwhelmed how many carriers you have available
Reabsorption rises with the filtered load until the transporters reach their aggregate capacity.

questions.note:
**In uncontrolled diabetes the filtered glucose load is higher than the proximal tubule's transport maximum, so the excess spills into the urine.**

Hyperglycemia causes increased tubular glucose secretion: false. Glucose isn't secreted; it's filtered and reabsorbed.

The tubular glucose concentration exceeds the Tmax for glucose reabsorption: true. Once every SGLT carrier is busy, extra glucose stays in the tubule (slide 14).

Tubular glucose reabsorption is inhibited by ibuprofen: false. Ibuprofen is a distractor here; it doesn't block glucose transport.

Filtration fraction for glucose is increased by ibuprofen: false. NSAIDs, if anything, lower GFR, and that wouldn't explain glycosuria.

Glomerular injury is leading to increased glucose filtration: false. Glucose is already freely filtered; the problem is the load, not a leaky barrier.

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old woman is seen in the nephrology clinic to review recent laboratory results that are as follows:

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the best estimate of her creatinine clearance?

evidence.quote: The clearance, um, times the plasma concentration of your substance is equal to the urine concentration of that substance times its flow rate.
so you can remember C equals UV over P.
creatinine is a byproduct of muscle metabolism, and it's cleared almost entirely by filtration.

questions.note:
**Clearance is U × V / P, with V as a flow rate, so a 24-hour volume has to be divided by 1440 minutes first.**

The work: V = 1440 mL / 1440 min = 1 mL/min. C = (50 mg/dL × 1 mL/min) / 2 mg/dL = 25 mL/min.

25 mL/min: true. Matches the calculation above.

30 mL/min: false. Too high; U × V / P gives 25.

35 mL/min: false. Too high; U × V / P gives 25.

40 mL/min: false. Too high; U × V / P gives 25.

45 mL/min: false. Too high; U × V / P gives 25.

50 mL/min: false. That's U × V with the plasma creatinine left out (or P taken as 1).
